z-m-18-01.title: If there are two equations, is the solution always one pair?
z-m-18-01.topic: Systems of linear equations with no solution or infinitely many solutions
z-m-18-01.goal: Confirm through checking a solution, judging information, and examples you make yourself that when two linear equations with two unknowns are put together, the solution falls into three cases (one pair, none, infinitely many), and explain under what condition which case occurs.
z-m-18-01.material:
Soyoung said, "If there are two linear equations with the two unknowns x and y, there is always exactly one pair (x, y) that satisfies both equations at once." Here x and y can be any numbers, and the equations are all linear equations with integer coefficients. Soyoung wants to check her idea with the system of equations below. How to read: 'x plus 2y equals 6', '2x plus 4y equals 10'.
  ㉠ x + 2y = 6
  ㉡ 2x + 4y = 10
z-m-18-01.thinking.0: Finding and fixing the line in a solution where the conclusion comes out without grounds
z-m-18-01.thinking.1: Judging what more information is needed to decide the number of solutions
z-m-18-01.thinking.2: Making several equations yourself that satisfy the conditions and checking them
z-m-18-01.thinking.3: Sorting out the conditions under which a claim of 'always' holds
z-m-18-01.prereq.0: Knowing that a solution of a linear equation with two unknowns is a pair (x, y)
z-m-18-01.prereq.1: The meaning of a solution of a system of equations (a pair that satisfies both equations at once)
z-m-18-01.prereq.2: Experience of seeing a linear equation ax+by=c as a line on the coordinate plane (grade 8 level; you do not need to know the relation to the number of solutions)
z-m-18-01.s.s1.prompt: In the solution below, which Soyoung wrote out for ㉠ and ㉡, choose one line where the grounds for drawing the conclusion are lacking. Set aside the first idea (Soyoung's statement) for now and check line by line whether the equations really hold.
z-m-18-01.s.s1.hint.0: Put (0, 0) into the left side of equation ㉠, x + 2y = 6, and check whether it becomes 6.
z-m-18-01.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether in line 2 the same 2x + 4y can be equal to both of the numbers 12 and 10 at the same time.
z-m-18-01.s.s1.line.0: Multiplying both sides of ㉠ x + 2y = 6 by 2 gives 2x + 4y = 12.
z-m-18-01.s.s1.line.1: Comparing this equation with ㉡ 2x + 4y = 10, the left sides are the same but the right sides differ, 12 and 10.
z-m-18-01.s.s1.line.2: Therefore x and y both disappear, so x = 0, y = 0 is the solution.
z-m-18-01.s.s1.line.3: So the solution of this system of equations is the one pair (0, 0).
z-m-18-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 does not follow. In line 2 it came out that the same 2x + 4y would have to be both 12 and 10, which means it cannot be satisfied by any values of x and y. 'x and y disappeared' does not mean 'x and y are 0.' If you put (0, 0) into ㉠, you get 0 = 6, which does not hold. Line 4 is a conclusion that carries over line 3's mistake.
z-m-18-01.s.s2.prompt: Leave ㉠ as it is and change ㉡ to 2x + 4y = c. (c can be any number, and we do not yet know its value. How to read: '2x plus 4y equals c') With only what you know now, what can you say about the solution of this system of equations?
z-m-18-01.s.s2.hint.0: Write the equation you get by multiplying both sides of ㉠ by 2 and compare it side by side with the form of ㉡.
z-m-18-01.s.s2.hint.1: Put in 12 and a number other than 12 for c, one each, and test whether the two equations become the same condition.
z-m-18-01.s.s2.o.a: Whatever c is, the solution is always decided as one pair
z-m-18-01.s.s2.r.a: This is a choice that brought over the first belief that two equations mean one pair. You did not check that the left side 2x + 4y is 2 times that of ㉠.
z-m-18-01.s.s2.o.b: Whatever c is, there are no x, y satisfying both equations
z-m-18-01.s.s2.r.b: You declared 'they can never meet' looking only at the left side of ㉡. You did not consider whether, depending on the value of c, the two equations could become the same equation.
z-m-18-01.s.s2.o.c: We need to know the value of c. Depending on c, there is no solution or infinitely many
z-m-18-01.s.s2.o.d: If c is 12 there is no solution, and for any other c there are infinitely many
z-m-18-01.s.s2.r.d: You found the two cases but the pairing is reversed. Write out for yourself whether ㉡ becomes the same equation as ㉠ when 2x + 4y is 12, 2 times 6.
z-m-18-01.s.s2.explain: The left side of ㉡, 2x + 4y, is 2 times the left side of ㉠. If c = 12, ㉡ is ㉠ with both sides doubled, so they are the same condition and there are infinitely many solutions, and if c is not 12, the same 2x + 4y would have to be a value different from 12, 2 times 6, so there is no solution. For this system of equations, there is no value of c for which the solution is exactly one pair. So to talk about the number of solutions, you need the value of c.
z-m-18-01.s.s3.prompt: Now design a system of equations with ㉠ x + 2y = 6 that has no solution at all. Write the new equation as ax + by = c, and make two different equations. (a, b, c are integers, a and b are not 0 and each has absolute value at most 20, and c has absolute value at most 100. 'ax + by = c' is read 'a x plus b y equals c'.)
z-m-18-01.s.s3.hint.0: Recall what happened in s2 when c was not 12, and compare what relation the coefficients of x and y had with ㉠ then.
z-m-18-01.s.s3.hint.1: Decide a and b first, then change c and test one by one whether there is an (x, y) that satisfies both that equation and ㉠. You must leave out the c that makes it the same equation as ㉠.
z-m-18-01.s.s3.ok.c1: a, b, c are all integers.
z-m-18-01.s.s3.fail.c1: a, b, c must be integers.
z-m-18-01.s.s3.fail.c2: a and b must not be 0 and have absolute value at most 20, and c must have absolute value at most 100.
z-m-18-01.s.s3.ok.c3: The coefficients of x and y have the same ratio as ㉠ (the coefficient of y is 2 times the coefficient of x).
z-m-18-01.s.s3.fail.c3: Look at whether there is the same relation between the coefficients of x and y as in ㉠. With this form, the lines meet at one point.
z-m-18-01.s.s3.ok.c4: The constant on the right is not the same multiple as in ㉠ (it is not the same equation).
z-m-18-01.s.s3.fail.c4: This equation becomes the same equation as ㉠, so there are infinitely many solutions. For there to be no solution, the constant on the right must be different.
z-m-18-01.s.s3.explain: With (a, b, c) = (1, 2, 5), x + 2y would have to be both 6 and 5, so there is no solution. (2, 4, 7) and (-3, -6, -4) are the same. (2, 4, 12) is 2 times ㉠, so it is the same equation, and (1, 3, 4) has a different relation between the coefficients of x and y, so the lines meet at one point. Equations that represent the same line, like (2, 4, 7) and (4, 8, 14), are counted as one.
z-m-18-01.s.s4.prompt: Answer Soyoung this way. When is the statement 'If there are two equations, the solution is always exactly one pair' right and when is it wrong? Write the cases in which the solution is one pair, none, or infinitely many, connecting them to the form of the equations (the coefficients and the constant on the right).
z-m-18-01.s.s4.hint.0: Pair the equations you made in s2 and s3 with ㉠ one by one, and compare how many times ㉠ the coefficients and the constant on the right are.
z-m-18-01.s.s4.hint.1: Divide them into the pairs that had no solution, the pairs that had infinitely many solutions, and the pairs that had one pair, and write down what was different about each.
z-m-18-01.s.s4.placeholder: e.g., If the coefficients of x and y in the two equations are ..., then ...
z-m-18-01.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Did you write separately from what form of equations the no-solution case and the infinitely-many case each arise?
z-m-18-01.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Did you also write when only one pair comes out?
z-m-18-01.s.s4.selfAssess.2: Did you give number examples as evidence, like the equation you made in s3 or ㉠, ㉡?
z-m-18-01.s.s4.model.0: Soyoung's statement is not always right. If the ratio of the coefficients of x and y differs between the two equations, the solution is one pair. If the ratio of coefficients is the same but the ratio of the constants differs, there is no solution. If the ratio of the constants is the same too, it is the same equation, so there are infinitely many solutions. For example, x+2y=6 and 2x+4y=10 have no solution.
z-m-18-01.s.s4.model.1: You can think of them as two lines. If the slopes differ, they meet at one point, so the solution is one pair. If the slopes are the same and where they pass is different, they are parallel and never meet, so there is no solution. If they overlap completely, there are infinitely many solutions. So just because there are two equations, it is not always one pair.
z-m-18-01.s.s4.modelNote.1: An answer from the graph point of view. Instead of expressing it with coefficients and constants, it said the same thing using slope and 'where the line passes.'
